title: RFK Jr. proposes FDA look the other way on unproven peptides, report says
gist: The FDA under Health Secretary RFK Jr. has sent an "Interim Access Policy" on peptides to the White House for review; according to the AP, it would let the agency use "enforcement discretion" so compounding pharmacies could make unproven peptide drugs that FDA scientists flagged as risky in 2023. A Kennedy-reshaped advisory panel, most of whose new members have ties to the peptide industry, has already recommended putting six peptides back on the compounding list, and CSPI is pushing back.

insights.claim: The FDA has submitted an "Interim Access Policy" on peptides to the White House for review. People familiar with it say it would give the agency "enforcement discretion" not to enforce current peptide restrictions, which would reassure specialty pharmacies that want to make the drugs that they will not be targeted.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: This could open a quick, unregulated revenue channel for compounding pharmacies and peptide sellers without a formal approval.
insights.quote: it would give the FDA “enforcement discretion” on certain peptide drugs
insights.locator: The FDA submitted an “Interim Access Policy”

insights.claim: Formally adding the peptides back to the FDA's compounding list requires federal rulemaking that could take years and several rounds of public comment. The proposed enforcement discretion could stand in for that rulemaking or provide access while it is under way.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Enforcement discretion is the near-term catalyst for the timing of peptide market access, not the slow rulemaking.
insights.quote: The new proposed enforcement discretion could ease access in lieu of that rulemaking or provide access during the process.
insights.locator: It’s unclear if the FDA will

insights.claim: It is still unclear whether the FDA will act on its advisory panel's recommendation to put the peptides back on the compounding list.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Regulatory uncertainty persists, so any bet on peptide compounders depends on what the FDA actually does next.
insights.locator: It’s unclear if the FDA will

insights.claim: In 2023, FDA scientists found that a dozen popular injectable peptides lacked safety and efficacy data and posed risks, and the peptides were removed from the list of drugs compounding pharmacies may make.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: The scientific record against these products creates liability and reversal risk for anyone selling them.
insights.quote: In 2023, FDA scientists determined that the peptides lacked data on safety and efficacy and posed risks.
insights.locator: The proposal comes as the FDA

insights.claim: Unproven peptide drugs have kept growing in popularity despite the FDA restrictions, with sellers claiming without evidence that they improve appearance, boost energy and help heal injuries. They are especially popular in the Make America Healthy Again movement, where many prominent figures sell peptide products.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: A wellness market driven by politics and influencers is growing whatever the regulators say.
insights.quote: many prominent MAHA figures sell peptide products
insights.locator: Still, the dodgy drugs have grown

insights.claim: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. calls himself a "big fan" of peptides and promised on taking office to end what he called "FDA's war" on peptides.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
entities: Department of Health and Human Services
insights.so_what: Top-level political backing makes it more likely that peptide restrictions will be loosened.
insights.quote: Kennedy, a self-proclaimed “big fan” of peptides, vowed to end “FDA’s war” on peptides upon taking office.
insights.locator: Still, the dodgy drugs have grown

insights.claim: In June, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. appointed nine new members to the 13-member FDA advisory panel reviewing peptides, and at least six of them have ties to peptide-related businesses and clinics. In July, the panel voted to put six of the first seven peptides it considered back on the compounding list, overruling FDA staff scientists.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: The panel's conflicts of interest expose any approvals to legal and political challenge and to reversal later.
insights.quote: Of the new members, at least six have ties to peptide-related businesses and clinics, raising significant conflict-of-interest concerns.

insights.claim: The Center for Science in the Public Interest wrote to Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas urging him to disregard the peptide panel's recommendations. Its president, Pete Lurie, warned that letting them stand would allow "charlatans" to put consumers at risk of serious injury.
insights.speaker: Pete Lurie
entities: Center for Science in the Public Interest
insights.so_what: Organized opposition means more litigation and reputational risk for companies in the peptide supply chain.
insights.quote: If this conflicted committee’s recommendations stand, charlatans will continue to put unsuspecting consumers at risk of serious injury
